paragraphs.text: Lesson 7, Driving and Directions.
Conversation number 1, Driving.
Listen to Elizabeth and Jonas talk about a road trip.
Hey, Jonas.
How was your road trip to Chicago?
It was a nightmare, one disaster after another.
Huh?
What on earth happened?
Well, I offered to give my girlfriend's brother a ride to Philadelphia.
It was a bit out of her way, but that wasn't the problem.
The problem was that he's a super annoying backseat driver.
Really?
Yeah, like getting on my case for forgetting to use my turn signal before merging.
Or telling me that I should get out of the exit only lane.
On and on for about four hours.
My mom is like that.
I mean, it's okay that she reminds me to buckle up, but I wish she wouldn't scream, slow down.
Every time I go a tiny bit over the speed limit.
Exactly.
So after we dropped him off in Philly, we got stuck in a major traffic jam for over an hour
before I finally managed to get off the highway and take a different road.
And then there was a detour due to road work, and we got lost for another three hours.
Wow, that's nuts.
Was it pretty smooth sailing after that?
No, it gets worse.
We made a pit stop outside of Cleveland, and I was in such a rush to use the bathroom that
I locked my keys in the car.
After shelling out $50 for a locksmith, we were back on the road.
But then the engine started overheating and I had to pull over.
Oh no.
I think I would have given up if I were you.
Yeah, but we were already over halfway there by that point, so I was determined to keep
going.
Just as we were getting to Chicago, another driver cut me off and I had to slam on the
brakes to avoid crashing into him.
Geez, I didn't know Chicago drivers were so aggressive.
Unfortunately, the woman behind me was talking on her cell phone and when I suddenly stopped,
she rear-ended me.
No way.
Was your car badly damaged?
Nah, it was just a fender bender.
By insurance we'll cover the repairs, but the whole trip was really stressful.
Next time, I'm just booking a flight.
Conversation Vocabulary and Phrases
In the beginning of the conversation, Jonas offers to give his girlfriend's brother a ride.
That means take him in the car.
If you want to offer someone a ride, you can use these phrases.
Do you need a ride?
Or do you need a lift?
I'll pick you up at.
To pick someone up means to take the person in your car.
I can drop you off at.
To drop someone off is when the person leaves your car.
Unfortunately, the brother is a backseat driver.
That's a person in the car who is not driving, but who criticizes the driver's abilities,
or who makes lots of suggestions and gives lots of tips for the driver to improve.
Here are some of the comments a backseat driver might make.
You don't want to be in this lane, it's exit only.
Roads are divided into lanes.
An exit only lane is one where the only option is to leave the highway.
You forgot to use your turn signal, or blinker, before merging.
Turn signal, or blinker, refers to the yellow or orange light on the sides of a car, used
to indicate the direction you plan to go.
Merge means to move from one lane into another.
Slow down, the speed limit is 55.
The speed limit is the maximum velocity permitted on that road.
Slow down means to drive slower, and speed up means to drive faster.
You missed your turn.
This phrase means you accidentally went past the place where you were supposed to turn right
or left.
Stop tailgating, it's not safe.
Tailgating means to follow the car in front of you very closely.
Everybody buckle up.
Buckle up means to put on your seatbelt.
It's getting dark, you should turn on your headlights.
Headlights are the lights on the front of the car.
During the conversation, a number of driving problems are mentioned.
For example, I got stuck in a traffic jam.
A traffic jam is when the traffic is stopped or slow.
There was a detour due to road work.
A detour is an alternate route.
And road work means maintenance or repairs on the road.
I got lost.
I locked my keys in the car.
The engine started overheating and I had to pull over.
Over heating means getting too hot.
And pull over means drive the car to the side of the road and stop.
I got a flat tire.
A flat tire is when the tire loses its air.
The car broke down.
Broke down means it had a mechanical problem and stopped functioning.
Another car cut me off.
This means another car drove in front of my car very suddenly.
Another car rear-ended me.
Rear-ended means it hit or crashed into the back of my car.
Conversation number two, asking for directions.
The Yankee Stadium, but she gets lost on the way, so she stops to ask for directions.
Excuse me, how can I get to Yankee Stadium from here?
You have to get on the highway, but you already passed the on-ramp.
So turn around and go back the way it came.
And just follow the signs for I-95 South.
Go about five miles on I-95 and get off at exit two A.
Could you show me on the map?
Sure.
You're here.
And the highway is here.
Exit two A is here.
Thanks a lot.
Could you tell me how to get to Yankee Stadium?
Yes.
Go past the gas station and turn left at the first light.
That's Walton Avenue.
Go straight down Walton until you hit east 164th Street.
And then...
Just a minute.
Let me write this down.
Okay.
Take Walton to east 164th Street and turn right.
If you see the mall, you've gone too far.
After you're on 164th, then take your second left onto River Avenue.
Your best bet for parking is at the corner of River and 162nd Street.
Sorry.
Could you repeat the part about River Avenue?
From 164th Street, you turn left onto River Avenue and just keep going until you see the
parking lot.
It's about four blocks and it'll be on your left across from a hotel.
Did you get all that?
I think so.
Thanks.
Thanks.
Conversation vocabulary and phrases.
To ask for directions, you can start with, excuse me, and then use these phrases.
How can I get to the Museum of Modern Art?
Could you tell me how to get to Grand Street?
Where is the nearest hospital?
Directions are often given with these verbs.
Go plus a direction.
For example, go right.
Go left.
Go straight.
Go east.
Go west.
Go north.
Go south.
We can also use the verb go plus a distance.
For example, go three blocks down the street, then turn left.
Go five miles on Route 25 W, then take Exit 16.
Turn right.
Turn left.
And turn around.
Take the second right.
Or take the third left.
We can also use take with the name of a road or public transportation.
For example, take Route 81.
Take Main Street north for about three miles.
Take the three train, then transfer to the F train at Fulton Street.
Take the bus towards Chinatown.
And we can also say stay on plus the name of the road to continue on the same street.
For example, stay on this road for about five miles.
Stay on the highway for another ten minutes.
When giving directions, it's helpful to use landmarks.
Those are obvious reference points.
For example, go past the big white church.
When you get to the clock tower, turn left.
If you see a shopping mall, you've gone too far.
Turn right at the next light.
Light means traffic light in this context.
Then you can describe the position of the destination by saying,
the destination will be on your left or on your right.
It will be across from a hotel.
It will be next to the hospital.
Or it will be on the corner.
